storySpine.startingBelief: B.Com and BBA are fundamentally different in all subjects.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student is comparing course lists for B.Com and BBA.
storySpine.observation: Found Business Organization & Management in both Semester I documents.
storySpine.focus: Understanding that title overlap exists but doesn't imply identical curriculum depth.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Evidence shows shared titles, so one must ask about differences in depth.
storySpine.changedAction: Replaces 'this is the same course' with a query about specific module depth.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Writes a formal enquiry email to the department requesting syllabus depth.
storySpine.channelExperience: Viewer sees an evidence-backed correction of a common degree-comparison assumption.

candidates.title: The Shared Title Truth
candidates.audienceGap: Belief that degree titles define subject exclusivity.
candidates.viewerChange: Understands that specific modules may overlap regardless of degree title.
candidates.concept: Comparing Semester I course lists from official documents.
candidates.payoff: Student frames an informed question for course counselors.
candidates.hlni: Business Organization & Management exists in both B.Com and BBA Semester I curricula (JOY University, 2025-26).
candidates.support: JOY University PDF, B.Com Accounting & Finance p.5 and BBA Entrepreneurship Management p.9.
candidates.interpretationRule: Documented overlap is limited to these specific programmes and semesters.
candidates.visibleProof: Comparison highlights identical rows in both official PDFs.
candidates.limitations: Does not imply identical assessment, career outcomes, or course content.

demonstration.input: Two official university course PDFs for 2025-26.
demonstration.observation: Same course title appears in both degree programmes.
demonstration.nextQuestion: How does the depth of this module differ for each?

storySpine.startingBelief: Choosing a degree is a final decision based on program prestige.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student is unsure which program aligns with their goals.
storySpine.observation: Task labels are vague without knowing the assessment criteria.
storySpine.focus: Separating task types from actual assessment requirements.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Knowing the task is useless without knowing how it is marked.
storySpine.changedAction: Drafts a three-column worksheet to audit actual course requirements.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Creates a structured question sheet instead of guessing based on prestige.
storySpine.channelExperience: Viewer learns to map requirements to evidence-based questions.

candidates.title: The Assessment Audit
candidates.audienceGap: Confusing degree prestige with specific assessment requirements.
candidates.viewerChange: Uses a structured audit to evaluate course content.
candidates.concept: Auditing task requirements to form specific enquiries.
candidates.payoff: Student prepares a list of concrete questions for department heads.
candidates.hlni: A task label alone does not specify output, grading, or feedback mechanisms.
candidates.support: Standard pedagogical method for course evaluation.
candidates.interpretationRule: Unanswered cells indicate areas for direct enquiry.
candidates.visibleProof: A filled-out worksheet showing specific gaps in knowledge.
candidates.limitations: This does not evaluate student aptitude or predict academic success.

demonstration.visibleInput: Task: Analyze annual report. Graded by: ?
demonstration.observation: Grading criteria and feedback mechanisms are unknown.
demonstration.nextQuestion: What specific criterion is used to assess this task?

storySpine.startingBelief: I must choose the same degree as my friend to feel prepared.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student feels pressure to align with a friend's choice.
storySpine.observation: Different tasks within the same subject interest them differently.
storySpine.focus: Identifying personal interest in specific task components.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Individual task preferences are more actionable than degree titles.
storySpine.changedAction: Records specific tasks they actually enjoy doing during a trial.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Explains to their friend why their individual preferences differ.
storySpine.channelExperience: Viewer feels empowered to choose based on personal task alignment.

candidates.title: The Task Journal
candidates.audienceGap: Belief that degree choice equals social alignment.
candidates.viewerChange: Recognizes individual task preferences are valid markers for investigation.
candidates.concept: Journaling task-specific engagement to guide research.
candidates.device: A personal diary or note-taking session.
candidates.payoff: Student develops a list of questions about their own areas of interest.
candidates.hlni: A short activity can identify where you need help or want to investigate further.
candidates.support: Constructivist learning theory regarding student interest alignment.
candidates.interpretationRule: Observations must lead to specific research questions, not degree labels.
candidates.visibleProof: A journal entry showing one specific sticking point.
candidates.limitations: Does not measure aptitude or predict long-term success.

demonstration.input: A short task: 'Create a simple marketing flyer'.
demonstration.visibleInput: Stuck on: How to measure visual effectiveness.
demonstration.observation: I find the design easy, but the analytics hard.
demonstration.nextQuestion: Where can I find resources to learn marketing analytics?

storySpine.startingBelief: I am not 'business-minded' enough for either degree.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student is worried they lack the 'right' skills.
storySpine.observation: Certain requirements are just checklist items, not personality traits.
storySpine.focus: Distinguishing between personal desire and actionable requirements.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Assumption of inability prevents checking actual, manageable requirements.
storySpine.changedAction: Lists requirements as 'to-verify' items rather than 'I can't'.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Checks eligibility criteria systematically instead of feeling shame.
storySpine.channelExperience: Viewer moves from self-doubt to objective verification.

candidates.title: The Requirement Check
candidates.audienceGap: Equating academic requirements with inherent ability.
candidates.viewerChange: Learns to treat requirements as verification tasks.
candidates.payoff: Student completes a concrete checklist of actionable items.
candidates.hlni: Appealing options and available options are separate questions; check unknowns.
candidates.interpretationRule: Unknowns are not disqualifiers, just next steps.
candidates.limitations: Does not change official eligibility rules or admission criteria.

demonstration.observation: I don't know the exact level required.
demonstration.nextQuestion: What is the specific minimum score needed for admission?

storySpine.startingBelief: I can guess which degree an assignment belongs to based on the task.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student is shown a random business task without a source.
storySpine.observation: The task could plausibly exist in multiple business programmes.
storySpine.focus: Identifying the lack of evidence in isolated examples.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Without institutional proof, guessing is unreliable.
storySpine.changedAction: Refuses to label the task and asks for the source document.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Shows the teacher that information is missing.
storySpine.channelExperience: Viewer discovers the danger of guessing without sufficient source data.

candidates.title: The Unlabeled Task
candidates.audienceGap: Assuming single examples imply degree-specific content.
candidates.viewerChange: Learns to identify missing information before drawing conclusions.
candidates.concept: Presenting an unlabeled task to challenge assumptions.
candidates.payoff: Student successfully identifies what information is missing.
candidates.hlni: An unlabeled example cannot prove a degree-specific origin.
candidates.support: Logical reasoning regarding evidence and classification.
candidates.interpretationRule: If source evidence is absent, state 'Not Enough Information'.
candidates.visibleProof: A blank 'Source' column on a comparison chart.
candidates.limitations: Does not prove the task is absent from either degree.

demonstration.input: A card saying 'Draft a business model canvas'.
demonstration.visibleInput: Task: 'Draft a Business Model Canvas'. Degree?
demonstration.observation: No source information links this to a specific degree.
demonstration.nextQuestion: Which official document lists this as a requirement?

storySpine.startingBelief: High total credits mean a harder, better degree.
storySpine.studentSituation: Student compares credit totals of two different programmes.
storySpine.observation: Totals are identical, but subjects are completely different.
storySpine.focus: Understanding that aggregates hide underlying content.
storySpine.whyQuestionFollows: Aggregates are misleading; only component breakdown reveals truth.
storySpine.changedAction: Requests a breakdown of the credit totals.
storySpine.visibleConsequence: Compares subject lists rather than totals.
storySpine.channelExperience: Viewer discovers why totals aren't the whole story.

candidates.title: The Total Illusion
candidates.audienceGap: Using aggregates to judge degree quality.
candidates.viewerChange: Understands that component breakdowns are necessary for comparison.
candidates.concept: Using arithmetic to show how totals can be misleading.
candidates.payoff: Student avoids making decisions based on total credit counts.
candidates.hlni: Aggregates hide underlying components; always ask for a breakdown.
candidates.interpretationRule: Never conclude similarity from an equal total.
candidates.visibleProof: Two lists with the same sum but different items.
candidates.limitations: Clearly illustrative; does not refer to real credit counts.

demonstration.input: Two charts showing 120 total credits each.
demonstration.observation: The components making up the 120 are totally different.
demonstration.nextQuestion: What is the breakdown of these credits by subject?

plan.contrast: Trust uses official curriculum evidence to debunk title assumptions; Connection uses personal journaling to help individuals navigate interest; Discovery uses an unlabeled example to teach critical evaluation of missing data.

issues: insight: In 'The Task Journal' concept, the student explains their preferences to a friend, but the concept lacks a clear link between this conversation and an academic outcome. Correction: Change the visible consequence to the student using their task-specific notes to draft a query for a course counselor, focusing on how specific modules support those interests.

integrity: The 'Discovery' concept uses a business model canvas as an example, which is a generic business tool, but does not provide a mechanism to verify if such a task exists in the specific JOY University documents previously mentioned. Correction: Include a step in the Discovery concept where the student compares the unlabeled task against the official Semester I documents (ju-bcom-af-2025-sem1, ju-bba-em-2025-sem1) to check if the task is explicitly mentioned.

issues: integrity: In trust_001, the visibleConsequence is 'Writes a formal enquiry email to the department requesting syllabus depth', which is a passive action that does not demonstrate the student's improved decision-making. Correction: Change the visibleConsequence to showing the student using the syllabus depth information to actively select between two elective module options.

fidelity: In connection_001, the whyQuestionFollows claims individual task preferences are more actionable, but the visibleConsequence is only 'Drafts a query for a counselor', which does not show the actionable result of the preference. Correction: Modify the visibleConsequence to show the student choosing a specific module based on the task preference identified in their journal.
